hints: Think about the journey of blood: where is pressure highest (just after leaving the heart's ventricles) and where has it lost most energy by the time it returns?

Remember the rule that pressure falls continuously along a circulation, so veins are much lower than arteries, and the very end of the long systemic circuit back to the right atrium is the lowest point of all.
walkthrough:
**Start where pressure is made**

Blood pressure is created by the ventricles contracting. So pressure is highest in the arteries that leave the heart directly.

Think: aorta leaves the strong left ventricle, pulmonary artery leaves the right ventricle.

**Follow how pressure is lost**

As blood flows further from the heart, friction and branching into smaller vessels use up energy. So pressure drops steadily along arteries to capillaries to veins.

Rule to remember: arteries > capillaries > veins in pressure.

**Compare the two veins**

Both C pulmonary vein and D vena cava are veins, so both are low pressure. But the vena cava is at the very end of the long systemic circuit, just before blood re-enters the right atrium.

By then almost all pressure has been lost, so its pressure is close to zero and lower than in the shorter pulmonary circuit. That makes D the answer.

options.A: Incorrect. The aorta receives blood directly from the left ventricle, so it has the highest pressure in the body, not the lowest.
options.B: Incorrect. The pulmonary artery is still an artery leaving the right ventricle, so its pressure is much higher than in any vein.
options.C: Incorrect. The pulmonary vein is low pressure, but it carries blood over the short lung circuit back to the left atrium, so its pressure is still higher than in the vena cava.
options.D: Correct. The vena cava returns blood from the body to the right atrium at the end of the systemic circuit, where pressure has fallen to its lowest value.
